stories.topic: The 1991 trade reforms were 30 years in the making
stories.summary: Amit argues that the 1991 reforms happened quickly, with no public consultation, so perhaps change can skip the slow pipeline. Ajay disagrees using customs duties. From the 1960s, through the work of Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Manmohan Singh's PhD thesis, economists argued fiercely about trade barriers against 'the lefties and the nationalists'. The data and research piled up, and the reformers won the debates conference after conference. By 1991, cutting duties from 350% to 5% was a settled question for many people. The only open question was how to sequence it. Ajay adds that the reforms that skipped this groundwork tended to work out less well.
stories.insight: Reforms that look overnight are usually the visible tip of decades of data, research and argument. That groundwork also produces the people who carry the knowledge, because 'the joint secretaries don't know much'.
stories.quote: But there were actually like 20 years of investment in the early stages of the pipeline that led to that simple clarity that trade barriers have to go.

stories.topic: From clueless about pension law to drafting inflation targeting
stories.summary: While describing the implementation stage of policy, Ajay offers a personal aside. When the New Pension System was being turned into law, he understood the idea but knew nothing about its legal scaffolding, so he could only watch as a spectator. By the time inflation targeting came along, he had learned enough to follow the whole path himself: from monetary economics, to drafting an agreement, to drafting a law.
stories.insight: Turning a good idea into reality needs very different skills at each stage. Even an expert economist had to learn the craft of legal drafting, which Ajay calls an 'exotic skill in India' because most laws here are poorly drafted.
stories.quote: I thought about the new pension system, but at the time I was clueless and I did not know what it meant in terms of its legal scaffolding.

stories.topic: Turning down Kirit Parikh: Ajay's biggest mistake
stories.summary: On another podcast, a friend asked Ajay without warning to name one mistake he had made in his life. He went back to age 21. Fresh out of IIT, the economist Kirit Parikh invited him to apprentice with him for a couple of years before doing a PhD. Ajay was dazzled by the idea of a PhD in the United States, so he declined and went abroad. He now calls it the dumbest decision imaginable.
stories.insight: Close apprenticeship with a great mind can beat the prestige of credentials. The glamour of a famous path can hide a better opportunity sitting right in front of you.
stories.quote: Like I could have had a couple of years apprenticing with him, like literally getting one-on-one time with him four times a week. And that would have been the greatest education in the world possible.

stories.topic: The hunter-gatherer paradise and the curse of agriculture
stories.summary: As children we are told that savage hunter-gatherers progressed to agriculture and then to industry. Ajay says modern thinking has turned this around. Hunter-gatherers were free, women were free, and health was good: male skeletons reached six feet and female skeletons five feet seven, heights not seen again until the 20th century. Agriculture brought disease, shrinking heights, social control and women treated as property. Grain also enabled early states, whose main dealings with the people were taxation and conscription. He describes the stretch from agriculture in Babylon about 5,000 years ago to liberal democracy in 19th-century UK as a long 'dark regress'.
stories.insight: Progress is not a straight line, and the story we grow up with can be badly wrong. For most of history the state was something to escape, not something that served you.
stories.quote: If you had to choose a year to be born into, you would always choose a hunter gatherer period.

stories.topic: The 20th century as a stress test of progress
stories.summary: Ajay suggests judging progress over the span of one life. Pick 20-year-olds and 60-year-olds at random from the 20th century, and for large numbers of them the rest of life went terribly: two world wars, the Russian Revolution, Nazi rule, the threat of communism and nuclear war. Weimar Germany's flowering of freedom in 1918 became Hitler in 1933. The hope of 1989 gave way to Putin's Russia, a near-miss in Poland and Hungary's decline. Deng Xiaoping's program from 1978 ended in Xi Jinping's one-man rule from 2012. Large-scale land war returned in 2022. India too began in 1947 with Gandhiji, Nehru, Tagore and Ramanujan, 'the star pupil' of the post-colonial world, and he asks the listener to look at where we've come.
stories.insight: Catastrophe is always possible, so you should never assume progress is locked in. Strive for it, but stay 'cold and careful and nervous' about the world.
stories.quote: Like we were the star pupil of what post-colonial experience was supposed to be. And you know, look at where we've come.

stories.topic: Three stages of Ajay's belief about persuasion
stories.summary: As a child, Ajay believed that showing someone how Kepler's laws follow from Newton's laws would instantly change the world and banish superstition. Then came decades of gloom, when he believed people only talk past each other, avoid conflict, and never change their minds. Now he holds a middle view. In a zone of truth and trust, people do hear each other. Nobody admits defeat, not even privately, but over time the mind mulls things over and shifts by about 10%.
stories.insight: Persuasion is real but slow, partial and hidden by ego. Expecting visible surrender sets you up for despair, while a 10% shift in ten people is a big win.
stories.quote: I will never be honest enough to say in front of you that you were right and I was wrong. Okay, this is my human frailty.

stories.summary: A mentor and boss at the Ministry of Finance had a clear career track mapped out for Ajay and was sure it was right. Ajay felt his real place was in the world of knowledge: reading and writing books, doing research, working with data and statistics. He followed that path and is surprised to have ended up in front of a camera on this show. He has also lived through the 'crushing humiliation and misery' of seeing his areas of work go horribly wrong, again and again.
stories.insight: Find the place where you are most useful, even if a respected mentor sees a different path for you. Then accept that the world owes you nothing, and keep building anyway.
stories.quote: But I always felt that the right path for me is in the world of knowledge, not in the world of action.

recommendations.item: Weapons of the Weak
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the episode, building on his argument that the move from hunter-gatherer life to agriculture was a decline.
recommendations.reason: It develops the view that states emerged to tax and conscript, and that many people sensibly tried to keep the state out of their lives. Ajay sees 'more than a shadow' of this in Indian society, where many people want to stay far away from the government.

recommendations.item: Against the Grain
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Mentioned in Ajay's recommendation as an earlier show recommendation and a source of his argument about agriculture and early states.
recommendations.reason: It explains why agriculture and grain-based early states made life worse for ordinary people, which overturns the childhood story of steady progress.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Amit notes that the show has recommended both Against the Grain and Seeing Like a State, making it 'very much a James C Scott fantasy'.
recommendations.reason: It is another James C Scott book the hosts value for understanding the state.

recommendations.item: Runaway
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, deliberately unrelated to the episode's themes, from his favourite living writer.
recommendations.reason: Munro's stories are set in one province of Canada yet capture the human condition so well that readers everywhere love her. Amit calls this collection a masterpiece.

recommendations.item: Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: Recommended alongside Runaway.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls both collections masterpieces and suggests them as a break from the state, economics and politics, because he believes every good work of fiction speaks to the reader personally.

recommendations.item: The Bear Came Over the Mountain
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: A short story published in The New Yorker, linked in the show notes and free to read.
recommendations.reason: It is perhaps Amit's favourite short story of all time, and he calls it 'just magnificent'.

recommendations.item: The Solution
recommendations.creator: Bertolt Brecht
recommendations.context: Amit reads it aloud after Ajay says the state should be the agent of the people but often becomes their ruler.
recommendations.reason: In a few lines it skewers a state that blames its people instead of serving them.

recommendations.item: Kashi Ka Assi
recommendations.creator: Kashinath Singh
recommendations.context: Amit quotes a line from it, in its family-friendly version, to frame the cynic's question: why care about the world at all?
recommendations.reason: Its line about playing your harmonium while the world goes to hell captures the temptation to withdraw, which Ajay then answers.

recommendations.item: The End of History?
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Amit cites it, noting the question mark, as the symbol of the optimism of 1989.
recommendations.reason: It captures the moment when liberal democracy seemed to have won for good. That assumption has since reversed, which Amit uses to question whether progress is inevitable.

recommendations.item: Mera Joota Hai Japani
recommendations.context: Amit plays it for listeners during the discussion of globalization.
recommendations.reason: He introduces it, playfully, as 'a famous song that is about the glory of globalization'.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: This episode was prompted by a question Amit asked at the end of The Reformers.
recommendations.reason: Amit thinks it is one of their best episodes because the story means so much to them both. It asks what drove reformers to fight for decades without reward.

recommendations.item: The Ideas of Our Constitution (Episode 164 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Madhav Khosla)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit cites Madhav Khosla's idea of the constitution's 'pedagogic' effect while critiquing top-down theories of change.
recommendations.reason: It lays out the transformative, top-down view of the Indian constitution that Amit argues against here.

recommendations.item: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit refers to it when asking Ajay to show 'the engine room' of how the state changes.
recommendations.reason: It shows Ajay working as an agent of change from inside the system, on pension reform.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit calls it his great episode with KP Krishnan in the same lead-in.
recommendations.reason: It traces what Ajay's group of reformers achieved over a long period of time.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit points listeners to the show's three episodes on the nature of the state.
recommendations.reason: It gives the background on what the state is, which the policy pipeline discussion builds on.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit singles out the second of the three state episodes during Ajay's account of market failures and low-coercion solutions.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it covers exactly how to think about policy: what the state should and should not do.

recommendations.item: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episode 27 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The third of the three episodes on the state that Amit points listeners to.
recommendations.reason: It completes the series that elaborates on what Ajay describes here.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions it when noting that universities don't do the work of imagining policy solutions.
recommendations.reason: It explains why the academy has stepped away from real-world problem solving.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as related viewing on how the state works.
recommendations.reason: It is further background on how the state actually behaves.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. The episode brings up the 2022 return of land war and jokes about Ukraine being 'content'.
recommendations.reason: It gives detail on the war Ajay cites as proof that catastrophe is always possible.

recommendations.item: XKDR Forum paper and software on methodology for nighttime lights data ('But clouds got in my way')
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay gives nighttime satellite lights as his example of measuring India from the sky.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says his group is at the global frontier of improving NASA's methods for processing this data. The data measures prosperity monthly at half-kilometre resolution without depending on the government.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on state capacity, governance and institutions (Episode 18 of Jack of All Knowledge)
recommendations.context: The podcast conversation where a friend asked Ajay, with zero notice, to name one mistake in his life.
recommendations.reason: This is where Ajay first told the story of turning down Kirit Parikh's apprenticeship offer.

core_ideas.concept: Separate the state from the people
core_ideas.explanation: Indians tend to be 'excessively statist' and blur the state, the people, and individuals into one thing, as in saying 'India won the World Cup'. Ajay argues the people matter more. Almost all wealth, truth, beauty and creativity comes from society, and so does most of the rot, such as the crushing of freedom. The basic question should be how people can build culture, associations, firms and clubs themselves, instead of always running to the mai-baap sarkar.
core_ideas.quote: Some bloke won some sports match. There is the people of India and there is the state. It's good to separate them.

core_ideas.concept: Change from below and from above: you need both
core_ideas.explanation: Amit once believed policy people would achieve nothing. His view was that you should work on the demand side of the political marketplace, the people, because the supply side, the state, responds to demand. He now thinks small changes on the supply side can have a massive impact, and that both are needed. Ajay gives two templates. Decriminalising homosexuality and recognising gay marriage were people-led: states followed opinion polls. Globalization in India was an elite, top-down project, because anti-foreigner feeling comes easily and the case for openness was clear mainly to thinkers and leaders like Vajpayee, Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram and Narasimha Rao.
core_ideas.quote: I think even small incremental changes at that supply end can have a massive impact on society.

core_ideas.concept: A liberal constitution as 'topsoil' cannot change society from the top
core_ideas.explanation: Ambedkar called the constitution a mere topsoil: a liberal document laid over a deeply illiberal society to keep it in check. Later scholars, such as Madhav Khosla with his idea of its 'pedagogic' effect, kept this top-down view. Amit argues it cannot work. Many people stopped trying to build a better society after independence, expecting the constitution and the state to do the job.
core_ideas.quote: Gandhi, I think, was wrong about many things, but one thing that he was certainly right about is that change has to come from within society, it has to come from the bottom up.

core_ideas.explanation: Critics of Big Tech are right about the problems: addiction machines, data harvesting, tribalism, echo chambers and polarization. But their usual answer, state regulation of algorithms, is dangerous. Once the state can tell companies what to do, that power will eventually be held by the worst possible person. Amit argues social problems must be solved socially.
core_ideas.quote: Because imagine that power in the hands of the worst person you can think of, and not some benevolent person who wants the good of everyone.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit notes that belief in progress rests on a tiny sample of centuries. Ajay suggests the timescale of one life. Much of the 20th century was catastrophic, the hopes of 1989 were betrayed, and democratic backsliding is now happening in country after country. Dream of progress and work for it, but don't fall into a 'millennial fervour' that assumes it is locked in.
core_ideas.quote: Social and political catastrophe is always possible.

core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on James C Scott, Ajay argues that early states existed mainly to tax and conscript. Their rulers wanted more people to control, so 'lines on maps' are a silly modern idea. People voted with their feet and ran away from states. Being stateless was better than living under a tyrannical state.
core_ideas.quote: Actually, what every tyrant wants is more people because if you control more people, you can oppress them.

core_ideas.concept: The policy pipeline: left to right, no skipping steps
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay describes how the state changes as a sequence of stages. (1) Data and measurement. (2) Research: refining 'crude oil' data into knowledge. (3) Imagining low-coercion solutions to genuine market failures, with several rival ideas, because 'when there is only one game in town, you have surely a bad thing going'. (4) A vigorous public debate that widens the Overton window, which needs free speech. (5) Expert committees that legitimize radical ideas. (6) Decisions, encoded in laws. (7) Implementation: drafting good laws and designing accountable organizations. Each stage needs very different knowledge, failure at any stage kills the reform, and the whole journey can take about 25 years.
core_ideas.quote: And there is no running away from this pipeline.

core_ideas.explanation: Without measurement, you are left with opinion and spectacle, and 'the guy with the biggest megaphone will win'. Building a measurement system, for example for air quality, takes about a generation. Ajay warns of a bait-and-switch: in a moral panic ('there is a crisis. Something must be done. X is something.'), frightened people accept authority, and the state rushes through its most oppressive measures.
core_ideas.quote: no amount of moral fervour or urgency can substitute for data.

core_ideas.concept: Satellites can measure what weak states won't
core_ideas.explanation: In poorer countries, government data suffers from incompetence and from suppression of unflattering numbers. Satellite imagery gets around both problems. For example, lights photographed at 1:30 a.m. come from street lights, petrol stations and commercial complexes. That gives a monthly map of prosperity at half-kilometre resolution. India's ISRO doesn't release such data freely, but other providers do.
core_ideas.quote: The bird in the sky sees the damn truth.

core_ideas.concept: Fame is a curse; common knowledge is usually wrong
core_ideas.explanation: When you put any field under the microscope, what famous people say loudly usually turns out to be wrong. Ajay also defends correlations, which parts of the economics profession look down on. Interpreted with care, they are a powerful path to insight.
core_ideas.quote: Everything that is loudly stated by all famous people is wrong. Okay, so fame is a curse. It interferes with information.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay judges every state intervention by its cost in money or coercion, and since all tax money is raised through coercion, the two are really the same thing. A good solution gets the job done substantively, even if only 60%, with the least coercion. It should assume realistic state capacity, which Ajay says is a euphemism for state incapacity.
core_ideas.quote: Ultimately the poison is coercion. The poison that the state drips on the people is coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Society changes one conversation at a time
core_ideas.explanation: Megaphone advocacy on social media 'gets precisely nothing done'. What changes minds is quiet, face-to-face conversation in a zone of truth and trust, and living as an example, because people do as we do, not as we say. Each good conversation shifts both sides by about 10%, and that adds up: persuading ten people by 10% on a couple of important things is a real achievement.
core_ideas.quote: What works is quiet, careful conversations from one to another.

core_ideas.concept: The world is interested in you, even if you aren't interested in it
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay answers the cynic who says 'let the world burn, I'll enjoy my life'. Even with zero altruism, self-interest demands that you understand politics and society. If you were in Weimar Germany, your job in 1918 was to hold off the nationalists, and in 1933 to take your loved ones and leave. Without a theory of the world, you get crushed when catastrophe comes.
core_ideas.quote: You may not be interested in the world, but the world is interested in you.

core_ideas.explanation: Idealists burn out by smashing their heads against 'some mad bugger's wall', often because they believe the world will be fixed quickly. The other extreme, apathy, is just as wrong. Ajay's alternative is to pace yourself, keep realistic expectations, treat the work as your dharma, and ask for no reward or success. We are pebbles in an avalanche. Accept defeat without becoming bitter or quitting.
core_ideas.quote: The highest superpower is the ability to keep going.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says the Indian elite is still at a 'crude credentialist transactional stage' of community. Real community means bonds of values and trust. Its members practise 'the Western way of war': write up the war diaries, celebrate successes, criticize failures harshly, cry together, and keep going. This avoids both collapse and the 'childish triumphalism' Ajay sees as common in India. Doing, failing and debating in this way is how knowledge builds up.
core_ideas.quote: meaning you have to be the person that tells me that I'm full of shit. That's the only way it'll ever work.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's exercise for looking honestly at yourself. Our ego insists we did everything right and the world did everything wrong. Imagining a letter to your younger self forces you to list what you would do differently, and with hindsight you find that almost everything could have been done better.
core_ideas.quote: That if I could write a letter that went in a time machine to the me of a certain year, what would I say?

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Right after Ajay defends the value of correlations, Amit offers one: total hours watched of Everything is Everything have been rising along with India's GDP, so 'the prosperity of our nation relies upon us.'

Amit's 'naughty thought': it's good that the world is going backwards, 'Because the creator economy is booming. And Ajay Shah, we need content.' Ajay replies: 'Like if there had been no war in Ukraine, what episode would you make?'

Ajay: 'In a good country, elected legislators write laws. In a bad country, the joint secretary writes the law.' Amit then pictures this episode playing on a giant screen to a hall full of protesting joint secretaries, adding: 'And you of all people with a broken ankle, you don't even have all your joints.'

Amit applies Ajay's 10% theory of persuasion: 'right after this recording, I am going to ask you for ten Diet Cokes. So you change your views by ten percent and give me one. Isn't that cunning of me?'
Ajay on Nazism: 'Nazi stands for nationalist socialism', calling it two bad ideas fused into one.

When Ajay says the art and beauty all come from the people, Amit interjects that the state 'can set up a commission to compose a sonata. They can set up a commission to come up with a new raga which is nationalistic.'

Amit claims he shifted the Overton window of podcast duration. His five- and six-hour episodes made two or three hours normal: when he started, 'one hour was considered a deep dive', and now 'one hour is like a miniature.'
Riffing on 'paradigms change one funeral at a time', Amit recalls Ajay's line that 'society changes one WhatsApp uncle at a time'.

Ajay opens with a line about the dialectic being interested in you even if you aren't interested in it. Amit asks him to explain it in simple English, and Ajay obliges: 'You may not be interested in the world, but the world is interested in you. There you go.'
Ajay on raw data without analysis: 'there is data, data everywhere, but not a thought to think.'

Bertolt Brecht's 'The Solution', read by Amit: after the 17 June uprising, leaflets on the Stalinallee said the people had lost the government's confidence. Brecht's reply: 'Would it not in that case be simpler for the government to dissolve the people and elect another?'
Mai-baap sarkar: the paternalistic idea of the government as parent, which both hosts say Indians run to by default.

Martin Luther King's 'the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice', and the saying that 'paradigms change one funeral at a time'. Amit uses both to question the assumption that progress is inevitable.
Francis Fukuyama's 'The End of History?' (1989, 'with the question mark'), along with the fall of the Berlin Wall and the Soviet Union, as the high point of liberal optimism.
Steven Pinker's 'the better angels of our nature', cited by Amit for the good side of our hardwiring that culture can amplify. Social media, by contrast, amplifies our 'worse demons' of tribalism.
Ajay's tribute to the scientific revolution: 'nature and her mysteries lay hidden in the night. God said let Newton be and all was light', followed by Maxwell's equations, relativity and Darwin.
Thomas Jefferson on the price of liberty being eternal vigilance, and Margaret Thatcher on battles you have to fight again and again, both cited by Amit.
'A republic, if you can keep it': Ajay recalls this answer from a framer of the US constitution but can't remember who said it. His point is that every generation has to fight for its freedom.
Gandhiji's 'be the change that you want to see in the world', which Ajay invokes for why change must start with us.

Amit quizzes Ajay on who said that he wasn't so smart, he just stayed with problems longer. Even with the clue 'he's one of your heroes', Ajay can't guess. The answer is Albert Einstein. Ajay adds that at 16 Einstein wondered what the world would look like riding a beam of light, and stayed with that question for years until it led to special relativity.
Amit's two perseverance quotes: Confucius, 'It doesn't matter how slowly you go, as long as you don't stop', and Vivian Greene, 'don't wait for the storms to pass, learn to dance in the rain'.
From Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi, in its 'family friendly version': 'Bhaad mein jaaye duniya, hum bajaayein harmonium'. The world is going to hell, but I'm going to play my harmonium.

Amit's running gag of crediting 'Robi-da, my favourite philosopher'. He cites Robi-da's song about treading a path of 'ekla cholo', and later says 'Shob kichu, shob kichu. Everything is everything, as a great Robi-da would say.'
Mera Joota Hai Japani, which Amit plays as 'a famous song that is about the glory of globalization'.
